newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Storm clouds loom over Asian economies - report.
newsitem.headline: Storm clouds loom over Asian economies - report.

text.p: Asian economies might face tough times unless they find ways to boost productivity and overcome resistance to reforming key areas like the financial and banking sectors, a report has warned.

"The key drawbacks in Asia are human and physical infrastructure inadequacies and systemic shortcomings that may have been easy to overlook during the early days of industrialisation," said the Asian Intelligence report of the Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy (PERC).

The report, a copy of which was made available on Sunday, said Asian economies will bounce back in 1997 from the doldrums this year, but this could derail efforts to implement what may be unpopular economic reforms.

"It is not simply a matter of buying the latest machine or technology for a factory in order to get more output out of each worker, although that is exactly what many economic managers in Asia think is the problem," the report said.

It noted that companies in the U.S. and Europe have evolved in such a way that they now can routinely rely on an extensive network of service outfits who must "work smart" to distinguish themselves from the competition.

"In short, companies in the U.S. and Europe can pursue productivity enhancement policies more easily that can many companies in Asia because there is a critical mass of support services readily at hand on which to draw," the PERC said.
Another issue Asia must tackle is the strong resistance to fundamental changes in the running of critical sectors of its economies, it said.
Japan, which is often touted as a model of Asia's economic success, is now being hobbled by structural problems in a banking industry burdened by tens of millions of dollars in bad debt.

The PERC report singled out South Korea, which has just been invited to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) as representative of countries in the region highly resistant to reforms.

The PERC warned: "Korean exports may pick up in 1997, but unless the country's antiquated financial sector is reformed drastically, the country's entire industrial structure will be growing off a very shaky base."
While banks in the United States and Europe are undergoing painful restructuring to remain competitive and survive, most Asian banks are "standing still -- none more so than in Korea."

"Yet pressure is building to open up Asian financial markets to more foreign competition," the report said, adding, "if that happens, the resulting shakeout of Asian financial institutions could be traumatic."
The report said countries like Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia are now focusing more on their services sectors and taking a close look at measures to enhance productivity.

The PERC suggested that economic success should not be judged by sharp growth in gross domestic product (GDP) alone and that companies should take a look at factors like new foreign investment in a particular nation's services sector.
